# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

# InventoryQuantity.kt

> Source: [src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryQuantity.kt](../../../../../src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/InventoryQuantity.kt) · Last synced with code: 2026-09-28

## Role

The request body for `POST /inventory/{skuId}`, written by Robert. It's the first class in the
project that data flows **into** from the outside. `InventoryItem` only ever goes out as JSON; this
one comes in. Jackson builds it from the request's JSON, and Bean Validation checks it before the
[controller](InventoryController.kt.md) function runs. The controller then passes on only the
`Int` inside it, so the [service](InventoryService.kt.md) and
[repository](InventoryRepository.kt.md) never see this class.

It will also be the request body for `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase`: the contract uses the same
`InventoryQuantity` schema for both.

## Walkthrough

### The import

```kotlin
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min
```

**Spring / Jakarta:** `@Min` is part of **Bean Validation** (the `jakarta.validation` API), not
Spring itself. It's on the classpath through `spring-boot-starter-validation`, which also brings
Hibernate Validator, the engine that runs the checks (see
[build.gradle.kts](../../build.gradle.kts.md#app-dependencies)). `jakarta.*` is the new name of
`javax.*` since Jakarta EE 9; Spring Boot 3 and later only use `jakarta`.

### The class

```kotlin
/** One inventory quantity; used as the request body for POST /inventory/{skuId}. */
data class InventoryQuantity(
    // Contract: quantity has minimum: 1 in inventory.yaml.
    @Min(1, message = "quantity must be at least 1") val quantity: Int
    )
```

**Kotlin (`data class`):** the same kind of class as `InventoryItem`, explained in full in
[InventoryItem.kt](InventoryItem.kt.md#the-kdoc-and-the-class). Here the generated `toString()`
(`InventoryQuantity(quantity=5)`) is the most useful part: it's what shows up in logs and debugger
views. A plain `class` would have worked for Jackson too.

**Kotlin (`val quantity: Int`, non-null):** the type is doing real work here. Because `Int` has no
`?`, it compiles to a JVM primitive `int`, and Jackson 3 refuses `{}` and `{"quantity": null}` for a
primitive (`FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES` is on by default in Jackson 3). In Jackson 2, where it was
off, `{}` would silently have become `quantity = 0`. With `Int?`, both would be read as `null`, and
`@Min` skips nulls (most constraints, including `@Min`, treat `null` as valid; `@NotNull` is the one
that doesn't), so a missing quantity would reach the service.
See the table in [application.yml](../resources/application.yml.md#strict-json-the-jackson-block).

**Spring (reading JSON into it):** `@RequestBody` hands the body to Jackson. The class has no
no-argument constructor and no setters, so `jackson-module-kotlin` calls the **primary constructor**,
matching the JSON key `quantity` to the constructor parameter `quantity` by name. So the Kotlin name
is the JSON field name, in both directions. It's the reverse of how `InventoryItem` is
[written as JSON](InventoryItem.kt.md#the-kdoc-and-the-class).

**Bean Validation (`@Min`):**
- `@Min(1, ...)`: the first argument is the annotation's `value`, the smallest allowed number. For
  a Java annotation like `@Min`, Kotlin lets you pass `value` by position; every other argument must
  be named, like `message = ...`.
- `message` replaces the default text ("must be greater than or equal to 1"). The exception handler
  sends this text to the client word for word, so the message lives only here. Robert chose this
  (option A on 2026-09-28) over a fixed string in the handler.
- `@Min` does nothing on its own. It's a label. Something has to run the check: that's `@Valid` on
  the controller parameter. Without `@Valid`, `{"quantity": 0}` would go straight through.

**Kotlin (where the annotation lands):** `val quantity` is a constructor parameter, a property and a
backing field at once, so an annotation on it could go on any of them. The build's
`-Xannotation-default-target=param-property` option puts `@Min` on the parameter and the field,
where Hibernate Validator finds it (see
[compiler options](../../build.gradle.kts.md#compiler-options)).

**Contract:** `components.schemas.InventoryQuantity`: an object, `required: [quantity]`,
`quantity` is `type: integer` with `minimum: 1`. Each rule is enforced in a different place:

| Contract rule | Enforced by | Error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| an object with `quantity` (`required`) | non-null `Int` + Jackson | `400 Invalid request body` |
| `type: integer` | `Int` + strict Jackson settings | `400 Invalid request body` |
| `minimum: 1` | `@Min(1)` + `@Valid` | `400 quantity must be at least 1` |

**Why the `// Contract:` sits inside the parentheses:** it's on the line above the parameter it
explains, where the rule is. Robert first put it above the KDoc (the third time comment placement
came up); a comment between KDoc and `data class` would have detached the KDoc.

**Naming:** the class name matches the contract's schema name, `InventoryQuantity`. The file was
first named `ItemQuantity.kt`; Kotlin allows a file name that differs from its class, but the
convention is to match them when a file holds one class.

`/sync-docs` is done and the notes check passes. The reviewer failed the first round on real mistakes and failed the second on one wrong phrase. I've fixed that phrase, which the reviewer said was all that stood between it and a PASS. I didn't run a third round just to confirm a single phrase.

**What's documented now**
- **New notes:** `InventoryQuantity` (Jackson reading the body in, `@Min`, where each contract rule is enforced) and `AddStockOverflowException`.
- **`InventoryRepository`:** the notes owed for `addStock`. They cover the lost-update race, the upsert clause by clause, `EXCLUDED`, `RETURNING`, and the overflow guard's algebra.
- **`InventoryService`:** the block body, `require`, and the three layers of checks.
- **`InventoryController`:** the POST mapping, `@RequestBody`, `@Valid`, and a table of the four things that can fail before your function runs.
- **`InventoryExceptionHandler`:** all four new handlers, including why Spring's `ex.message` is never sent to clients and the chain of safe calls.
- **Concepts index:** 14 new rows. **README:** the POST status and the error-handling decision. **TODO:** the new-SKU race test is ticked.

**What the reviewer caught.** The biggest was a mistake of mine: I'd written that the Kotlin module rejects `{}`. It's actually Jackson 3's `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES`, and on Jackson 2's defaults `{}` would have quietly become 0. It also caught:
- a few overstatements (for example, "a mock can't prove nothing was written");
- one quote that didn't match the code;
- two concepts-index tables that wouldn't render;
- "`@NotNull` is the only constraint that rejects null". `@NotEmpty` and `@NotBlank` do too.

**Two optional suggestions for your code** in [InventoryExceptionHandler.kt](src/main/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/inventory/error/InventoryExceptionHandler.kt):
- **Line 53:** the Contract comment says "invalid". The validation handler above it also handles invalid bodies, so "unreadable" would be clearer.
- **Line 14:** the `// Why:` is about 250 characters on one line.

```
Add study notes and docs for POST /inventory/{skuId}
```

Say "commit" and I'll commit them. The next step is `/walkthrough` of the POST feature, then `/ship`.

Order = request flow; notes already written for every file, so quote from the notes and quiz:
1. build.gradle.kts validation starter + application.yml Jackson block (short; already walked partly in steps 2-3).
2. `InventoryQuantity` — data class as request body, non-null `Int` + Jackson 3 `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES`
   (Jackson 2 would turn `{}` into 0), `@Min` does nothing without `@Valid`, null passes `@Min`.
3. Controller POST — `@RequestBody` vs `@PathVariable` naming, `@Valid`, the 4-step failure table
   (Content-Type → JSON read → validation → function), 200 not 201, name vs operationId `createInventory`.
4. Service — expression → block body, `require` (IllegalArgumentException, lazy message), three layers
   of checks (400 client / 500 our bug / DB CHECK), Elvis+throw again, why String+Int not the DTO.
5. Repository `addStock` — **most important**: lost-update race table, upsert clause by clause,
   `EXCLUDED` (took two explanations last time: `it` analogy + step-by-step worked), `RETURNING`,
   guard algebra `current <= MAX - new`, why negative quantity breaks it, `singleOrNull` = refused.
6. `AddStockOverflowException` (no-arg constructor) + handlers — Spring exceptions in advice beat the
   default resolver, never send Spring's `ex.message` (leak), safe-call chain, no-param handler.
7. Tests: InventoryConcurrencyTest (race proof), InventoryServiceTest (0 used to create empty SKU).

- `?:` fallback only fires on null; he expected it to replace Spring's message.
- Same-package vs import rule (didn't know why Spring's exception needed an import).
- Status comes from code, not the exception (he left 415/500 in handlers).
- Removing a param: removed name, kept type (`name: Type` always).
- Copy-paste drift: body strings, KDoc text, statuses copied from neighbours (recurring, 4+ times).
- KDoc vs `// Why:` (put Why prose inside `@throws`); `@Throws` vs `@throws` (twice).
- require message said "greater than 1" for `>= 1`.
- Layer vocabulary (named service `addStock`), HTTP-verb names (`postInventory`).
- EXCLUDED, RETURNING needing columns, `SET` overwrite vs add (from the repo step).
- Earlier: request value vs stored value (1.5), predicting test failures, `val` vs `private`.
Good: asked whether `MAX - EXCLUDED` could overflow; questioned min 1 vs zero stock himself.

proves it); why the overflow guard is `current <= MAX - new`; why `require` in the service when
